System software operates the hardware (OS, compilers, assemblers, loaders). Application software runs on top of the system
software. Handwritten BH p.1


 Translator (language processor): software that converts a program written in one language (the source language) into an
 equivalent program in another language (the target language). A computer understands only machine language, so
 translators bridge human-readable code and machine-executable instructions.

 Translator: source language → target language. A compiler reports errors during translation.


Three types of translator Teacher handout: Unit-1 :


 Compiler: translates the whole high-level program into machine (or assembly) code before it runs. It is fast at run time, but
 debugging is a little harder. Examples: C, C++, Java (to byte code).
 Interpreter: takes the source program and its input and executes it directly, statement by statement, without producing an
 object file. Examples: Python, JavaScript.
 Assembler: translates low-level assembly code into machine code. It is the fastest of the three. A single-pass assembler
 does this in one scan; a multi-pass assembler uses several scans.

Cousin Role

 Preprocessor Runs before compilation. Processes macros ( #define ) and file inclusion ( #include ) and produces the
 modified source code.

 Compiler Translates the modified source into an assembly-language target program, reporting errors.

 Assembler Translates the assembly program into relocatable machine code (object code).

 Linker Large programs are compiled in pieces. The linker joins the object files with library files and resolves external
 references (for example calls to printf ), giving the final target file.

 Loader Reads the relocatable machine code, adjusts the relocatable addresses and loads the target code into memory
 for execution.



 The handwritten notes BH p.1 label the assembler output as “object codes / target code or absolute machine code” and
 the linker output as “relocatable machine code (final target file)”. The teacher handout gives the usual textbook order:
 assembler → relocatable machine code, linker → executable, loader → absolute addresses in memory. Write the textbook

 What is the need for a symbol table? What attributes are stored in it?

 A symbol table is a data structure (array, linked list or, usually, a hash table) with one entry per identifier in the program.
 It is created by the lexical analyzer and used by every later phase.

 Need: (1) store each name once so all phases share it; (2) semantic analysis checks declarations, scope and types from it;
 (3) intermediate and target code generation get each variable’s type, size and address from it; (4) it helps find errors such
 as undeclared or redeclared names; (5) fast lookup and insert.

 2.1 Tokens, Lexemes and Patterns

 Lexeme: the actual sequence of characters in the program that matches a pattern (e.g. key , 1.2 ).
 Token: the category (class) of a lexeme, passed to the parser as <token-name, attribute-value> (e.g. identifier, number,
 keyword).
 Pattern: the rule, usually a regular expression, describing which lexemes belong to a token (e.g. identifier = [a-zA-Z_]
 [a-zA-Z0-9_]* ).


Typical tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants/numbers, strings, operators, special symbols (punctuation). White space and
comments are not tokens; the scanner discards them. Attributes are given mainly to identifiers (a pointer to the symbol-table
entry: is it a variable or function name, its type …) and to numbers (their value).

 3.4 Recursive-Descent Parsing (Predictive, no backtracking)
A recursive-descent parser has one procedure per non-terminal. Each procedure looks at the current input symbol (lookahead)
and chooses the production whose right side can start with it, then calls the procedures of the right side in order; match()
checks a terminal and advances. When the choice is always unique from one lookahead, there is no backtracking: this is a

A bottom-up parser builds the parse tree from the leaves (the input) up to the root. At each step it finds a substring that

 LR(0) item: a production with a dot in its right side. The dot shows how much has been seen. A → •XYZ (nothing seen), A →
 X•YZ, A → XY•Z (shift items), A → XYZ• (complete: reduce). For A → ε the only item is A → •. “Dot = yet to be read” (BH
 p.20).


Augmented grammar: add S' → S, so that accepting = reducing S' → S (item S' → S• on $).
CLOSURE(I): start with I; for every item A → α•Bβ in it and every production B → γ, add B → •γ; repeat until nothing new.
GOTO(I, X): CLOSURE of all items A → αX•β such that A → α•Xβ is in I. Only an item set not seen before becomes a new state
(BH p.20).
Canonical collection: I0 = CLOSURE({S' → •S}); apply GOTO on every symbol after a dot until no new states appear. The states
and GOTO edges form a DFA.

LR(0) table: GOTO on a terminal a from Ii to Ij ⇒ ACTION[i, a] = shift j; GOTO on a non-terminal A ⇒ GOTO[i, A] = j; if A → α• ∈
Ii (A ≠ S') ⇒ ACTION[i, a] = reduce A → α for every terminal a and $; if S' → S• ∈ Ii ⇒ ACTION[i, $] = accept. Any cell with two
actions is a conflict ⇒ not LR(0).

 LR(1) item [A → α•β, a]: an LR(0) item plus a lookahead terminal a. A reduce by A → α is done only when the next input is

 3.10 LALR(1) Parser
LALR(1) (Look-Ahead LR) = build the LR(1) collection, then merge states with the same core (same LR(0) items), taking the
union of the lookaheads (“identify common, lookahead may be different”, BH p.26). GOTO edges are redirected to the merged
states. Number of states = SLR’s number of states (much smaller than CLR); power between SLR and CLR. YACC builds LALR
parsers.

 Merging never creates a shift-reduce conflict that was not already in CLR (shift entries do not depend on lookahead).
 Merging can create a reduce-reduce conflict (two merged states with complete items on the same lookahead). Then the
 grammar is LR(1) but not LALR(1): solved in End-Sem Dec 2025 Q5(A) below.

 3.11 Operator-Precedence Parsing
The handwritten notes do not cover this lecture (lecture 14); this section follows the slide deck
operator_precedence_parsing_slides_corrected.

 Operator grammar: a grammar in which (1) no production has ε on the right side and (2) no right side has two adjacent
 non-terminals. Example: E → E+E | E*E | (E) | id is an operator grammar; E → EAE | id, A → + | * is not (E A E has adjacent
 NTs), but substituting A gives the operator grammar above.


Between pairs of terminals three precedence relations are defined: a ⋖ b (a yields precedence to b: shift), a ≐ b (same
precedence: they belong to the same handle, e.g. ( ≐ )), a ⋗ b (a takes precedence over b: reduce). Non-terminals are ignored
when comparing; only the topmost terminal on the stack is compared with the input.

Building the relation table with LEADING and TRAILING
LEADING(A): terminals that can be the first terminal of a TRAILING(A): terminals that can be the last terminal.
string derived from A.
 A → αa or A → αaB ⇒ a ∈ TRAILING(A)
 A → aα or A → Baα ⇒ a ∈ LEADING(A) A → αB ⇒ TRAILING(B) ⊆ TRAILING(A)
 A → Bα ⇒ LEADING(B) ⊆ LEADING(A)

Relations from each production A → X1X2…Xn: (1) Xi, Xi+1 both terminals, or Xi, Xi+2 terminals with a non-terminal between
⇒ Xi ≐ Xi+1 (or Xi+2). (2) Xi terminal followed by non-terminal B ⇒ Xi ⋖ every b ∈ LEADING(B). (3) non-terminal B followed by
terminal Xi+1 ⇒ every a ∈ TRAILING(B) ⋗ Xi+1. (4) $ ⋖ LEADING(S) and TRAILING(S) ⋗ $.

Parsing algorithm
 1. Push $; append $ to the input. Let a = topmost terminal on the stack, b = current input symbol.
 2. If a = b = $: accept.
 3. If a ⋖ b or a ≐ b: shift b.
 4. If a ⋗ b: reduce: pop symbols until the topmost terminal on the stack is ⋖ the terminal most recently popped; the popped string is the

Precedence functions
The relation table (n × n) can be replaced by two functions f and g (2n numbers): a ⋖ b ⇔ f(a) < g(b), a ≐ b ⇔ f(a) = g(b), a ⋗ b
⇔ f(a) > g(b). Algorithm: (1) make nodes fa and ga for every terminal a (merge fa, gb if a ≐ b); (2) if a ⋗ b draw fa → gb; if a ⋖ b
draw gb → fa; (3) if the graph has a cycle, the functions do not exist; otherwise f(a) = length of the longest path from fa, g(b) =
length of the longest path from gb. Worked out in the End-Sem Nov 2023 Q5(a) and Re-Exam Feb 2025 Q7(c) answers below.

 PAST PAPER · End-Sem Dec 2025 (CSBS) · Q1(b) 5 marks

 Explain the rules of the CLOSURE() and GOTO() functions.

 CLOSURE(I) for a set of LR(0) items I: (1) every item of I is in CLOSURE(I); (2) if A → α•Bβ is in CLOSURE(I) and B → γ is a
 production, add B → •γ (if not already there); (3) repeat (2) until no new item can be added. For LR(1) items: from [A →
 α•Bβ, a] add [B → •γ, b] for every b ∈ FIRST(βa).

 GOTO(I, X) for a grammar symbol X: take every item A → α•Xβ in I, move the dot over X to get A → αX•β, and return the
 CLOSURE of this set. It is the transition of the LR DFA on X.

 Example (S' → S, S → CC, C → cC | d): CLOSURE({S' → •S}) = {S' → •S, S → •CC, C → •cC, C → •d}. GOTO(I0, C) =
 CLOSURE({S → C•C}) = {S → C•C, C → •cC, C → •d}. GOTO(I0, c) = {C → c•C, C → •cC, C → •d}. GOTO(I0, d) = {C → d•}.

 LR(k): L = the input is scanned from Left to right; R = the parser produces a Rightmost derivation in reverse; k = the

 1. Augment G with S' → S.

3. Canonical collection C: I0 = CLOSURE({S' → •S}). For each set I in C and each grammar symbol X with GOTO(I, X) non-

 (a) if A → α•aβ ∈ Ii, a a terminal, and GOTO(Ii, a) = Ij: ACTION[i, a] = shift j;

Why symbolic labels are needed. Intermediate code uses labels such as L1, L2, Lnext instead of final addresses. When a jump is
generated, the instruction it jumps to may not be emitted yet, so the compiler emits an incomplete jump. After code generation the
labels are tied to instruction positions and the targets are resolved. Backpatching is the systematic way to fill these in, and it avoids a
separate full pass just to repair forward jumps. Backpatching is also used for languages with complex control structures.

 What is a flow graph? Explain its role in code optimization.
 A flow graph is a directed graph whose nodes are the basic blocks of a program (maximal straight-line pieces of TAC with
 one entry and one exit) and whose edges show possible flow of control: Bi → Bj if Bj can run immediately after Bi (Bi
 jumps to Bj's leader, or Bj follows Bi and Bi does not end in an unconditional jump). Built by: find leaders (first statement,
 jump targets, statement after a jump) → split into blocks → add edges.

 Role in optimization: (1) inside each block, local optimizations (CSE, constant folding, dead code via DAG) are safe; (2) the
 edges let global data-flow analysis (reaching definitions, live variables, available expressions) find global CSE and dead

 elimination give the biggest gains; (4) blocks with no path from the entry are unreachable and are removed; (5) register
 allocation works per block and per loop. Here, constants a = 10, b = 20 propagate: c = 30, d = 60, so d > 50 is always true;

 PAST PAPER · Re-Exam Feb 2025 (CS) · Q7(b) 5 marks

 What are the problems (issues) in the design of a code generator?

 1. Input to the code generator — the IR (TAC, quadruples, trees, DAG) plus symbol-table types and addresses; assumed
 error-free with type conversions already inserted. Integer vs float operations need different instructions.
 2. Target program — absolute machine code (runs directly), relocatable code (separate compilation, needs
 linker/loader) or assembly (needs assembler); RISC vs CISC architecture.
 3. Memory management — mapping names to run-time addresses (static area, stack offsets) and labels to instruction
 addresses.
 4. Instruction selection — choosing good instructions; e.g. a = a + 1 → INC a instead of load/add/store.
 5. Register allocation and assignment — which values stay in registers and which register each gets; spills when
 registers run out; optimal assignment is NP-complete.
 6. Evaluation order — the order of computing sub-expressions changes the number of registers needed; must not
 change meaning.

 Overall goal: correct code first, then efficient code that respects the target machine.

 (2) Register allocation and assignment
 Registers are the fastest storage but few. Allocation chooses the set of variables kept in registers at each point;
 assignment picks the specific register for each. When no register is free, a value is spilled to memory and reloaded later,
 which costs time. Next-use/liveness information shows when a register's value is dead and the register can be reused.
 Finding an optimal assignment is NP-complete; machines may impose rules such as register pairs (e.g. a multiply puts its
 result in an even/odd pair).

 6.4 Introduction to Global Data-Flow Analysis

 Data-flow analysis collects information about how values are defined and used along all paths of the flow graph. For each
 block B we compute IN[B] (at entry) and OUT[B] (at exit) from equations of the form

 with IN/OUT of neighbouring blocks combined by ∪ (some path) or ∩ (all paths). The equations are solved iteratively until
 nothing changes.

 Explain storage allocation strategies.
 1. Static allocation — names are bound to storage at compile time; the binding never changes, so locals keep values
 between calls. Fast and simple, but sizes must be known at compile time, no recursion and no dynamic data structures
 (FORTRAN 77, globals/statics in C).

 2. Stack allocation — storage is organized as a stack of activation records: a record is pushed at each call and popped at
 return; locals are reached by offsets from SP/FP. Supports recursion (each activation has its own record); locals lose their
 values on return; cannot hold data that must outlive the call (C, Java, Pascal procedures).

 3. Heap allocation — blocks are allocated and freed in any order on request (malloc/free, new/delete or garbage
 collection). Supports dynamic data structures and data that outlive their creator; slower because of free-list
 management, and suffers fragmentation, dangling pointers and leaks.

 Write a note on the compilation of object-oriented features.

 ⚑ FLAG This topic is not in the 26–27 course policy (Units 1–6). A complete answer is given so the question is not lost, but
 study it last.


 Object-oriented languages add classes, objects, inheritance, dynamic binding and encapsulation; the compiler maps them
 onto ordinary records, procedures and pointers:

 1. Classes and objects → records. Each object is a heap record holding its fields at fixed offsets; methods are compiled
 once as ordinary procedures with an extra hidden parameter this (the object's address). o.f becomes a load at
 offset(f) from o.
 2. Inheritance → prefix layout. A subclass record begins with the superclass's fields in the same order and appends its
 own, so a subclass object can be used wherever a superclass object is expected (same offsets).
 3. Dynamic binding → virtual method tables (vtables). Each class has a table of pointers to its methods; every object
 stores a pointer to its class's vtable. A call o.m() compiles to: load vtable pointer from o; load the entry at m's fixed
 index; call it with this = o. Overriding just puts a different procedure in the subclass's table.
 4. Name mangling and overloading. Methods with the same name but different parameter types get unique internal
 names (e.g. Shape_area_int ); the type checker resolves overloading at compile time.
 5. Constructors/destructors. new C(…) → allocate the record on the heap, store the vtable pointer, call the
 constructor; destructors or garbage collection free it.
 6. Encapsulation (private/protected) is checked at compile time by the semantic analyzer; no run-time cost.

 class Sq : Shape { int s; int area(); }; t2 = t1[0] ; slot of area
 Shape *p = new Sq; p->area(); param p ; this
 call t2, 1 ; runs Sq::area
